title: Digit Lab
context: Grade 4, after comparing is secure. An adult sees a puzzle about arranging digits. What the page is actually doing is teaching one rule with one exception, and the exception is the whole lesson: zero cannot lead, because a number that starts with zero has quietly lost a place.

writeup.why: Build the biggest and the smallest number you can from a handful of digit cards, and find out where a zero is allowed to go.
writeup.look: A rack of digit cards along the bottom and a row of empty slots above it waiting to be filled.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Digit Lab' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the card slots filled against the card slots the target asks for, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each card lands and dropping back by one when a card is lifted out again; on the fourth phase it carries the steps taken instead, up and down counted separately, so a step back is never shown as a step undone. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The target strip runs across the top of the working area, 1086 by 56 at 64,202, one line in ink saying the greatest or the smallest and how many places the number must have, with the places drawn as that many small empty boxes at its right end so the target can be counted as well as read. Under it the card slots, up to six of them, 120 wide by 150 tall with a gap of 18, laid as one row at 64,274 and each carrying its place name in small ink underneath, so a card dropped in can be read for what it is worth as well as for what it is; the leading slot is drawn with a heavier outline than the rest. The stepper is a strip 1086 by 72 at 64,448: two round controls 72 across at its centre, one up and one down, with the number one less written to their left and the number one more to their right as each is made. The rack runs along the foot, 1086 by 182 at 64,548, holding the digit cards face up at 96 by 126 each, the digit 72 tall in ink on the paper colour, and a card lifted out leaves its outline behind in the rack so the set given stays countable. Sort the rack slides the cards still in it into increasing or decreasing order without lifting any of them. A zero dropped into the leading slot is refused: the outline shakes twice, a note 300 by 64 writes itself in the strip directly beneath saying that a number cannot begin with zero, and the zero then slides sideways along the row into the second slot by itself, any cards already standing to its right stepping one place along to let it in, so the number keeps all of its places. Repeat a card is a control 180 by 56 at the right end of the rack; pressing it and then a card lays an identical card beside it in the rack, drawn with a doubled outline so a clone is never mistaken for a card that was given. A step across a row of nines turns each nine over to a zero in turn, right to left, and the last carry opens one more card slot at the leading end if it has to. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a number is asked for, and on the third phase a choice pad of the rack's own cards as large keys in the same rectangle, so the card to be repeated can be chosen with one press instead of being dragged. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a digit takes the colour of its period, deep blue in the ones period, green in the thousands and vermilion in the lakhs, and rose in the millions where the international chart reaches; a digit under discussion, or the one that decides a comparison, is amber; a zero holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a place is told by its column heading and a period by its band before either is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the greatest and the smallest number the child built from the same set, with the zero's place marked on the smaller one.

phases.win: the slots fill in decreasing order and the target strip clears
phases.does: drags the largest card to the leftmost slot and carries on down
phases.goal: decreasing order puts the largest digit where it is worth the most
phases.says: Which card is worth most at the front? Put that one first.
phases.check: Away from the screen: you have the cards seven, two and nine. Which goes at the front, and why that one?
phases.feels: one card decides most of the answer, and it is the one at the front
phases.hands: Write six digits on six pieces of card, shuffle them face down, and have the child lay them out to make the biggest number they can, saying out loud why each card goes where it goes.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which card in the rack is the largest? Second rung, the phase's: which slot is worth the most? Third rung: the rack is cut to three cards with three slots and the child builds the greatest from those. The pad stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: counting starts small, and the cards come to hand in the order they happen to lie in the rack.
wrong.move: builds from the smallest card upward and fills the leftmost slot last.
wrong.screen: the number the child built stays in the card slots and a second row of the same cards is laid under it in decreasing order; the two rows are read out place by place from the left, the place names under the slots lighting as each pair is read. Neither row is taken away.

wrong.why: worth the most and last place have both been said about digits, and the ones place is where counting ends.
wrong.move: puts the largest card in the last slot because it is worth the most.
wrong.screen: that same card is carried along the row from the right to the left one slot at a time, and the place name under each slot lights with what the card would be worth standing there, the number growing as it travels.

phases.screen: six cards in the rack and six empty slots above
phases.soWhat: Decreasing order from the left gives the greatest number.
phases.concept: The greatest number you can make from given digits

phases.win: the zero settles into the second slot and the number keeps all its places
phases.does: tries the zero in the leading slot, is refused, and moves it along
phases.goal: a zero cannot lead, so it takes the second place
phases.says: Try the zero at the front. Read out loud what you made.
phases.check: Why is a number written with a zero at the front not really a six digit number?
phases.feels: the one card you were surest about is the one card that is not allowed there
phases.hands: Give the child a set of digit cards with a zero among them, ask for the smallest number, and let them put the zero at the front. Then read out loud what they have made and count its places.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what did the leading slot say? Second rung, the phase's: which is the smallest card that is not a zero? Third rung: the leading slot is filled for the child and only the rest of the row is left open. The pad stays open.

wrong.why: increasing order says the smallest digit goes first, and zero is the smallest digit there is.
wrong.move: puts the zero at the front and reads the result as a six digit number.
wrong.screen: the leading slot shakes twice and writes its reason underneath, then the zero slides into the second slot on its own; the places are counted from the right and where the zero had been standing the count comes up one short and the leading place name goes dark. The child's number stays in the answer slot.

wrong.why: the zero is what caused the trouble, so the far end of the row looks like the safest place to put it.
wrong.move: sends the zero all the way to the end of the row to be rid of it.
wrong.screen: the number built that way is laid under the number with the zero in the second slot and the two are compared place by place from the left, the first place where they differ lighting amber. Both rows stay on the stage.

phases.screen: the same cards, with the target strip now asking for the smallest
phases.soWhat: Zero cannot lead, so the smallest digit that is not zero goes first and the zero takes the second place.
phases.concept: The smallest number, and where zero has to go

phases.win: the repeated digit is the largest one and the number is the greatest possible
phases.does: clones one card and arranges all six
phases.goal: the digit you repeat decides whether you get the greatest or the smallest
phases.says: You are one card short. Which one would you use twice?
phases.check: You need the smallest number and you are one card short. Which card would you use twice?
phases.feels: there are not enough cards, and you are allowed to make another one
phases.hands: Give five cards and ask for a number with six places. Wait through the complaint that there are not enough cards, and then ask which card they would write down twice.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many places does the strip ask for? Second rung, the phase's: how many cards are in the rack? Third rung: the target is cut to four places with three cards, so one repeat fills it, and the child chooses which. The card keys stay open.

wrong.why: the rack has an order of its own and the first card is the one nearest the hand.
wrong.move: repeats the first card in the rack rather than the largest one.
wrong.screen: the clone is laid beside its card with its doubled outline, the row is built, and the number it makes is set under the number the largest card would have made; the two are compared place by place from the left with the first place that differs lighting amber. Neither number is removed.

wrong.why: five cards fill five slots, and a row that has used every card looks like a row that is done.
wrong.move: leaves the sixth card slot empty and reads the number as finished.
wrong.screen: the small boxes at the end of the target strip are counted out against the card slots holding a card, and the one empty slot is left ringed with its place name lit beneath it; the repeat control lights and nothing else on the stage moves.

phases.screen: five cards in the rack but six slots waiting above
phases.soWhat: The digit you repeat decides whether you get the greatest number or the smallest.
phases.concept: Repeating a digit to fill more places

phases.win: both neighbours are read out and a row of nines rolls over correctly
phases.does: steps up once and down once and reads both neighbours
phases.goal: the successor is one more and the predecessor is one less
phases.says: Step up once, then down twice. Where did you land?
phases.check: What is one less than the smallest six digit number, and how many digits has your answer?
phases.feels: one step up and a whole row of nines turns over under your hand
phases.hands: Write a number ending in a run of nines on paper, ask for one more, then ask for one less, and have both neighbours written in on either side of it.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which way along the strip does one more go? Second rung, the phase's: which place does it change first? Third rung: a two place number ending in a nine is put into the slots and the child steps it up once. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the two words are learnt together and sound alike, and both of them mean a neighbour.
wrong.move: gives the predecessor when the successor was asked for.
wrong.screen: the number is laid on a short ruled strip with its two neighbours drawn either side of it, the one less at its left and the one more at its right, and the step the child took is walked out along the strip so its direction can be seen. The child's number stays in the answer slot.

wrong.why: one more has always touched the last place and left the rest of the number alone.
wrong.move: steps up from a row of nines and changes only the last digit.
wrong.screen: the step is taken again slowly: each nine turns over to a zero in turn from the right, handing one on to the place at its left, and when the run of nines is used up a new card slot opens at the leading end to catch the last carry.

phases.screen: a finished number with a stepper beside it
phases.soWhat: The successor is one more and the predecessor is one less, wherever the nines are.

writeup.delight: The second phase, the moment the zero is dropped into the leading slot. The slot refuses it: the outline shakes twice and the reason writes itself out underneath in words. Then the zero slides sideways along the row into the second slot on its own, and the leading slot is left standing open with its heavier outline, waiting for a card that is not a zero. Nothing is taken off the stage, nothing is marked, and the row still holds as many places as it did before. The voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase six digit cards lie face up in the rack along the foot of the working area and six empty card slots wait above them, with the target strip across the top asking for the greatest and saying how many places. On the second the same six cards are back in the rack, the card slots are empty again, the strip now asks for the smallest, and the zero card sits in the rack looking like any other. On the third only five cards lie in the rack with six card slots waiting, so one slot must go unfilled unless a card is cloned. On the fourth a finished number stands in the card slots with the stepper parked beside it. The running count at the top left holds the slots filled against the slots wanted, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the largest card in the rack, or the zero card, or the empty sixth slot, or the stepper's up control, gives one slow pulse while the voice says to read the strip first. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any cards, any number of places, with the repeat control unlocked and the stepper free to run. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on building the greatest and smallest numbers and on stepping by one.
voiceLines: A rack of cards and a row of empty slots. Read the strip first.
Which card is worth most at the front? Put that one first.
Try the zero at the front. Read out loud what you made.
You are one card short. Which one would you use twice?
Step up once, then down twice. Where did you land?
Same cards, a different target. Read the strip again.
Free play. Any cards, any number of places, repeat what you like.
Lay the cards back in the rack and sort them before you build again.
You found the one place a zero is not allowed to stand.

observations.why: The largest digit ends up where the places are worth the most.
observations.soWhat: Which digit goes at the front matters more than all the others together.
observations.observe: Laying the cards in decreasing order gave the greatest number every time.

observations.why: A number written with a zero at the front has quietly lost a place.
observations.soWhat: Zero can go anywhere in a number except at the very front.
observations.observe: The leading slot would not take the zero, and it said why.

observations.why: Nothing was thrown away; the cards only shuffled along by one.
observations.soWhat: The smallest number puts the smallest digit that is not zero first, and the zero next.
observations.observe: The zero moved along one slot and the number still had all its places.

observations.why: The repeated digit takes a front place, where it is worth the most.
observations.soWhat: Which digit you repeat decides whether you get the greatest number or the smallest.
observations.observe: One card short of the places wanted, repeating the largest card beat every rearrangement.

observations.why: Each nine has nowhere to go but back to zero, and it hands one on to its left.
observations.soWhat: The successor of a number full of nines is one place longer than it was.
observations.observe: One step up from a row of nines turned every one of them over at once.

source_tool.description: A rack of digit cards sits along the bottom of the stage and a row of empty slots waits above it. The child drags cards into the slots to build a number, and a target strip says what is being asked for, the greatest or the smallest, and how many places it must have. A sort control lays the remaining cards in decreasing or increasing order so the arrangement can be checked against the rule. The leading slot is the whole point: dropping a zero into it is refused, the slot shakes, and the reason is written out, after which the zero slides to the second slot on its own and the number rebuilds. When more places are asked for than there are cards, a repeat control clones one card, and which card it clones decides whether the result is the greatest or the smallest. A stepper beside the finished number adds or takes away one and shows the successor and predecessor, rolling a whole row of nines over when it has to.
source_tool.art_direction: A rack of digit cards, empty slots / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.
Drawn things, not abstract boxes: token tiles, place value charts with ruled columns, a number line with labelled ticks, digit cards that can be picked up, and lettered tiles for the Roman numerals.

A large number is always shown with its digits sitting in named places, with the period bands behind them and the commas drawn where the Indian system puts them. A bare numeral with no chart behind it is never used to teach place value.
Where tokens or blocks stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A place is told apart by its column label first and by its band colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a token or a place the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The ones period is deep blue, the thousands period is green and the lakhs period is vermilion, and those three bands are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The millions period is rose and appears only where the international chart does. A digit under discussion, or the digit that decides a comparison, is amber. A zero holding an empty place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a period is told apart by its band and its label before its colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Lay the cards back in the rack and sort them before you build again.
voice.onNext: Same cards, a different target. Read the strip again.
voice.opening: A rack of cards and a row of empty slots. Read the strip first.
voice.onFinish: You found the one place a zero is not allowed to stand.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any cards, any number of places, repeat what you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: The greatest number you can make from given digits
The smallest number, and where zero has to go
Repeating a digit to fill more places

placement.where: After real digit cards have been arranged on a table and a zero has already caused an argument. The tool is what refuses the zero and says why, which a table cannot.

answer_key.rule: Writing the digits in decreasing order gives the greatest number and increasing order gives the smallest, except that a zero cannot stand at the front, so it takes the second place after the smallest digit that is not zero. If more places are wanted than there are digits, repeat the largest digit for the greatest number and the smallest for the smallest. The successor is one more and the predecessor is one less.
answer_key.wrong: The cards are laid back into the rack and sorted into order in front of the child, so the arrangement can be read before it is built again. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Put the largest digit at the leftmost slot, where it is worth the most.
Carry on placing the next largest digit each time.
In decreasing order that is nine, six, five, three, two and zero.
items.question: Make the greatest number using 3, 0, 2, 6, 5 and 9, each card once.
items.checkpoint: Decreasing order always gives the greatest number.
items.misconception: Starting from the smallest digit and building the number the wrong way round.

steps: Increasing order would put zero at the front, and a number cannot start with zero.
So the smallest card that is not zero goes first, which is two.
The zero takes the next slot, then the rest in increasing order.
items.question: Make the smallest number using the same six cards, each once.
items.checkpoint: Zero cannot lead, so it moves to the second place.
items.misconception: Writing 0,23,569, which is really a five digit number wearing a zero.

steps: Six slots are waiting but only five cards are given, so one must be repeated.
For the greatest number, repeat the largest card, which is eight.
Now lay all six in decreasing order: eight, eight, seven, five, three, zero.
items.question: Using 5, 0, 7, 8 and 3, make the greatest six digit number.
items.checkpoint: Repeating the largest digit is what makes the number bigger, not rearranging.
items.misconception: Repeating the first card in the rack rather than the largest one.

steps: The successor is one more, so add one and get 14,918.
The predecessor is one less, so take one away and get 14,916.
On a number line they sit one step either side of it.
items.answer: The successor is 14,918 and the predecessor is 14,916
items.question: What are the successor and the predecessor of 14,917?
items.checkpoint: Successor is one more and predecessor is one less, always.
items.misconception: Swapping the two words and giving the predecessor when the successor was asked for.

items.question: Write the predecessor of the smallest six digit number.
items.final_answer: 99,999, because the smallest six digit number is 1,00,000

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: holds the digits given, each one draggable into a slot
says whether the greatest or smallest is wanted and how many places
lays the remaining cards in increasing or decreasing order
refuses a zero and writes out the reason before moving it
clones one digit when more places are asked for than there are cards
adds or takes away one and shows the successor and predecessor

teaching_notes: Give a set with a zero in it on the very first try, not the third. The zero rule is the whole difficulty of this topic and everything else is rearranging. When the leading slot refuses the zero, stop and ask why 0,23,569 is not a six digit number at all; that question teaches more than the rule does. Repeating a digit is a separate move, so ask how many places are wanted before any card is cloned. For the stepper, choose numbers that roll over, such as the greatest five digit number. The easy ones teach nothing at all.
generation_prompt: Build a digit arranging tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A rack of draggable digit cards along the bottom and a row of empty slots above it, with a target strip stating whether the greatest or the smallest number is wanted and how many places it must have. A sort control lays the remaining rack cards in increasing or decreasing order. The leading slot refuses a zero: the slot shakes, a written reason appears, and the zero then animates into the second slot and the number rebuilds. A repeat control clones one card when more places are wanted than there are cards, and the tool reports whether the cloned card was the right choice for the stated target. A stepper beside the completed number adds or subtracts one and displays the successor and predecessor, cascading correctly across a row of nines. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Read the target strip, then drag cards from the rack into the slots. Try putting a zero at the front and see what happens. If you are short of cards, repeat one. Then use the stepper to find the numbers one either side.
